Rehoboam is forbidden to fight Israel (verses 1–12)

A few kind words might have prevented Rehoboam's subjects from rebelling, but all the military power of his kingdom could not bring them back.

When God has made his purpose known to us, it is useless to fight against it.

Even people without genuine faith may sometimes show enough regard for God's word to be restrained from wrong actions they would otherwise be inclined to commit.

Priests and Levites find refuge in Judah (verses 13–23)

When the priests and Levites came to Jerusalem, faithful Israelites followed them.

People whose hearts were set upon seeking the Lord God of Israel left their ancestral land and moved to Jerusalem.

They wanted free access to God's altar and freedom from the temptation to worship the golden calves.

What is best for our souls is best for us.

In every decision, we should give spiritual advantages a higher priority than outward convenience.

God's faithful people should seek fellowship with his faithful ministers.

When we demonstrate willingness to give up worldly interests as far as Christ and his gospel require, we have evidence that we truly are his disciples.

It also benefits a nation to protect true religion and people devoted to it.

Verses 1-12
A few good words might have prevented the rebellion of Rehoboam's subjects; but all the force of his kingdom cannot bring them back. And it is in vain to contend with the purpose of God, when it is made known to us. Even those who are destitute of true faith, will at times pay some regard to the word of God, and be kept by it from wrong actions, to which they are prone by nature.
[2Chr.11.13-2Chr.11.23]
Verses 13-23
When the priests and Levites came to Jerusalem, the devout, pious Israelites followed them. Such as set their hearts to seek the Lord God of Israel, left the inheritance of their fathers, and went to Jerusalem, that they might have free access to the altar of God, and be out of the temptation to worship the calves. That is best for us, which is best for our souls; in all our choices, religious advantages must be sought before all outward conveniences. Where God's faithful priests are, his faithful people should be. And when it has been proved that we are willing to renounce our worldly interests, so far as we are called to do so for the sake of Christ and his gospel, we have good evidence that we are truly his disciples. And it is the interest of a nation to protect religion and religious people.

modern_osis:
Original heading

Rehoboam, forsaking the Lord, is punished.

Rehoboam is punished for abandoning God

Once Rehoboam became powerful enough to believe he had nothing to fear from Jeroboam, he abandoned even his outward profession of godliness.

It is common, and deeply regrettable, for people who appear eager to seek and serve God during danger, illness or fear of death to abandon religion after receiving merciful deliverance.

God soon brought trouble upon Judah to awaken the people to repentance before their hearts became hardened.

When Providence corrects us, we should acknowledge God's justice and our own guilt.

If humiliating circumstances produce a genuinely humble heart, the suffering has accomplished its purpose.

It may then be removed or changed in its character.

The more we compare God's service with other kinds of service, the more reasonable and easy it appears.

Do laws requiring self-control seem difficult?

The consequences of excess are far harder.

Serving God is perfect freedom. Serving sinful desires is complete slavery.

Rehoboam never possessed a stable inward faith.

He did not entirely reject God, but he also never set his heart on seeking him.

He failed to serve the Lord because he failed to seek the Lord.

He did not pray as Solomon had for wisdom and grace, consult God's word as his guide or follow its directions.

Religion mattered little to him because he never truly committed his heart to it.

He did wrong because he was never firmly resolved to do good.
classic_reading:
[2Chr.12.1]
Chapter 12
Rehoboam, forsaking the Lord, is punished.
--When Rehoboam was so strong that he supposed he had nothing to fear from Jeroboam, he cast off his outward profession of godliness. It is very common, but very lamentable, that men, who in distress or danger, or near death, seem much engaged in seeking and serving God, throw aside all their religion when they have received a merciful deliverance. God quickly brought troubles upon Judah, to awaken the people to repentance, before their hearts were hardened. Thus it becomes us, when we are under the rebukes of Providence, to justify God, and to judge ourselves. If we have humbled hearts under humbling providences, the affliction has done its work; it shall be removed, or the property of it be altered. The more God's service is compared with other services, the more reasonable and easy it will appear. Are the laws of temperance thought hard? The effects of intemperance will be found much harder. The service of God is perfect liberty; the service of our lusts is complete slavery. Rehoboam was never rightly fixed in his religion. He never quite cast off God; yet he engaged not his heart to seek the Lord. See what his fault was; he did not serve the Lord, because he did not seek the Lord. He did not pray, as Solomon, for wisdom and grace; he did not consult the word of God, did not seek to that as his oracle, nor follow its directions. He made nothing of his religion, because he did not set his heart to it, nor ever came up to a steady resolution in it. He did evil, because he never was determined for good.

modern_osis:
Original heading

Abijah overcomes Jeroboam.

Abijah defeats Jeroboam

Jeroboam and his people had deserved severe punishment for their idolatry and apostasy.

Henry understands the victory God permitted Abijah to win as an act of judgment against them.

Yet Abijah himself was not genuinely devoted to God, as his character in 1 Kings 15:3 shows.

He drew confidence from his people's faith, not from a faithful life of his own.

People who deny the power of godliness often boast in its outward form.

Many who have very little genuine faith themselves still value it in others.

Nevertheless, Judah did include many sincere worshipers, and its cause was more righteous.

Surrounded by danger, where could they look for rescue but upward?

What an extraordinary comfort it is that the way to God remains open.

They cried out to the Lord.

Earnest prayer is truly a cry for help.

They added a shout of faith to their prayer, and became more than conquerors.

Jeroboam escaped Abijah's sword, but God struck him.

No one escapes God's judgment.
classic_reading:
[2Chr.13.1]
Chapter 13
Abijah overcomes Jeroboam.
--Jeroboam and his people, by apostacy and idolatry, merited the severe punishment Abijah was permitted to execute upon them. It appears from the character of Abijah, [1Kgs.15.3] 1Ki 15:3, that he was not himself truly religious, yet he encouraged himself from the religion of his people. It is common for those that deny the power of godliness, to boast of the form of it. Many that have little religion themselves, value it in others. But it was true that there were numbers of pious worshippers in Judah, and that theirs was the more righteous cause. In their distress, when danger was on every side, which way should they look for deliverance unless upward? It is an unspeakable comfort, that our way thither is always open. They cried unto the Lord. Earnest prayer is crying. To the cry of prayer they added the shout of faith, and became more than conquerors. Jeroboam escaped the sword of Abijah, but God struck him; there is no escaping his sword.

modern_osis:
Original heading

Asa's piety, He strengthens his kingdom.

Asa seeks God and strengthens Judah

Asa wanted to please God and sought his approval.

Happy are those who live by that rule—not doing what seems right merely in their own eyes or in the eyes of the world, but what is right before God.

Experience teaches us that seeking the Lord is good.

It brings rest, whereas chasing the world brings only distress and frustration.

Asa discussed with his people how to use the peace God had given them well.

Together they decided that peace was no excuse for laziness or careless self-confidence.

A formidable army of Ethiopians invaded his kingdom.

God permitted the trial so that Asa's faith would be tested.

His prayer was short, but expressed genuine faith and confidence in God.

When we go forward in God's name, we have reason to trust that he will work everything for the good of those whom he favors.
classic_reading:
[2Chr.14.1]
Chapter 14
Asa's piety, He strengthens his kingdom.
--Asa aimed at pleasing God, and studied to approve himself to him. Happy those that walk by this rule, not to do that which is right in their own eyes, or in the eye of the world, but which is so in God's sight. We find by experience that it is good to seek the Lord; it gives us rest; while we pursue the world, we meet with nothing but vexation. Asa consulted with his people how to make a good use of the peace they enjoyed; and concluded with them that they must not be idle, nor secure. A formidable army of Ethiopians invaded Asa's kingdom. This evil came upon them, that their faith in God might be tried. Asa's prayer is short, but it is the real language of faith and expectation from God. When we go forth in God's name, we cannot but prosper, and all things work together for the good of those whom he favours.

modern_osis:
Original heading

The people make a solemn covenant with God.

Asa and the people renew their covenant

Full religious reform appeared so difficult that Asa had not dared undertake it until he received assurance of God's help and acceptance.

He and the people offered sacrifices of thanksgiving for past blessings and prayer for further mercy.

Under the gospel, our spiritual sacrifices are prayer and praise.

The people voluntarily entered a covenant to seek the Lord, with each person doing so earnestly.

What is true religion if not seeking God—inquiring after him and turning to him in every circumstance?

Religion is worth nothing to us unless it engages our hearts.

God requires the whole heart, or none of it.

Our devotion to God our Savior should be acknowledged and demonstrated solemnly and openly.

Anything done in hypocrisy is merely burdensome, empty labor.
classic_reading:
[2Chr.15.1]
Chapter 15
The people make a solemn covenant with God.
--The work of complete reformation appeared so difficult, that Asa had not courage to attempt it, till assured of Divine assistance and acceptance. He and his people offered sacrifices to God; thanksgiving for the favours they had received, and supplication for further favours. Prayers and praises are now our spiritual sacrifices. The people, of their own will, covenanted to seek the Lord, each for himself, with earnestness. What is religion but seeking God, inquiring after him, applying to him upon all occasions? We make nothing of our religion, if we do not make heart-work of it; God will have all the heart, or none. Our devotedness to God our Saviour, should be avowed and shown in the most solemn and public manner. What is done in hypocrisy is a mere drudgery.

modern_osis:
Original heading

Asa seeks the aid of the Syrians, His death.

Asa's misplaced trust and death

A prophet of the Lord faithfully rebuked Asa for making an alliance with Syria.

God is displeased when people distrust him and rely more heavily upon human strength than on his power and goodness.

It is foolish to lean on a broken reed when we have the Rock of Ages to support us.

To show Asa his folly, the prophet reminded him that he, of all people, had good reason to trust God, who had already proved such a powerful Helper.

Our many experiences of God's goodness make later distrust more blameworthy.

Yet see how deceitful our hearts can be!

When we have no other source of help and necessity drives us to God, we trust him.

But when other supports appear, we readily depend on them too much.

Asa became angry at the prophet's correction.

What can human beings become when God leaves them to themselves?

Asa abused his authority to persecute God's prophet and was then left to misuse it further by oppressing his own subjects.

Two years before his death, Asa developed a disease in his feet.

Using physicians was his duty.

His sin and folly lay instead in trusting those physicians as though they could give what only God could give.

During every conflict and suffering, we must especially examine our hearts, seeking wholeness toward God through faith, patience and obedience.
classic_reading:
[2Chr.16.1]
Chapter 16
Asa seeks the aid of the Syrians, His death.
--A plain and faithful reproof was given to Asa by a prophet of the Lord, for making a league with Syria. God is displeased when he is distrusted, and when an arm of flesh is relied on, more than his power and goodness. It is foolish to lean on a broken reed, when we have the Rock of ages to rely upon. To convince Asa of his folly, the prophet shows that he, of all men, had no reason to distrust God, who had found him such a powerful Helper. The many experiences we have had of the goodness of God to us, aggravate our distrust of him. But see how deceitful our hearts are! we trust in God when we have nothing else to trust to, when need drives us to him; but when we have other things to stay on, we are apt to depend too much on them. Observe Asa's displeasure at this reproof. What is man, when God leaves him to himself! He that abused his power for persecuting God's prophet, was left to himself, to abuse it further for crushing his own subjects. Two years before he died, Asa was diseased in his feet. Making use of physicians was his duty; but trusting to them, and expecting that from them which was to be had from God only, were his sin and folly. In all conflicts and sufferings we need especially to look to our own hearts, that they may be perfect towards God, by faith, patience, and obedience.

modern_osis:
Original heading

Jehoshaphat promotes religion in Judah, His prosperity.

Jehoshaphat teaches the law in Judah

Jehoshaphat found widespread ignorance among his people and worked to ensure they were well taught.

In every age, the public teaching of God's word is the principal means of promoting true godliness.

Through it, people are taught to understand, while their consciences are awakened and directed.

This chapter also describes Jehoshaphat's prosperity.

His large army was not what stopped neighboring nations from attacking Judah.

They were restrained by the fear of God, which came upon them as Jehoshaphat reformed the land and established a teaching ministry.

God's appointed ordinances are a kingdom's greater strength and security than soldiers and weapons.

Scripture continually calls us to notice God's hand in every event, yet few people take that call seriously.

Let everyone make use of the abilities they possess, being faithful even in small matters.

Establish the worship of God in your homes.

Caring for a family is an important responsibility.

Why should we not teach our families from the book of the Lord's law, as Jehoshaphat taught his people?

But live consistently.

Do not recommend one thing while practicing another.

Begin with yourselves.

Seek the Lord God of Israel, and then invite children and servants to follow your example.
classic_reading:
[2Chr.17.1]
Chapter 17
Jehoshaphat promotes religion in Judah, His prosperity.
--Jehoshaphat found his people generally very ignorant, and therefore endeavoured to have them well taught. The public teaching of the word of God forms, in all ages, the great method of promoting the power of godliness. Thereby the understanding is informed, the conscience is awakened and directed. We have a particular account of Jehoshaphat's prosperity. But it was not his formidable army that restrained the neighbouring nations from attempting any thing against Israel, but the fear of God which fell upon them, when Jehoshaphat reformed his country, and set up a preaching ministry in it. The ordinances of God are more the strength and safety of a kingdom, than soldiers and weapons of war. The Bible requires use to notice the hand of God in every event, yet this is little regarded. But let all employ the talents they have: be faithful, even in that which is little. Set up the worship of God in your houses. The charge of a family is important. Why should you not instruct them as Jehoshaphat did his subjects, in the book of the law of the Lord. But be consistent. Do not recommend one thing, and practise another. Begin with yourselves. Seek to the Lord God of Israel, then call upon children and servants to follow your example.

modern_osis:
Original heading

Jehoshaphat's alliance with Ahab.

Jehoshaphat's alliance and rescue

This history has already been recorded in 1 Kings 22.

Great wealth and honor offer many opportunities to do good, but they also carry many traps and temptations.

Those who eagerly seek riches in the belief that wealth will enable them to accomplish good often fail to understand Satan's schemes and the deceitfulness of their own hearts.

Who can harm those whom God protects?

Who can shelter those whom God has decided to judge?

Jehoshaphat remained safe in his royal robes, while Ahab was killed despite his armor.

The race does not belong automatically to the swift, nor the battle to the strong.

We should beware of becoming entangled in the worldly projects of wicked people, and be even more careful never to join their sinful undertakings.

Nevertheless, God can deliver his faithful people even from dangers they brought upon themselves through sinful choices, when they cry to him.

All hearts are in his hand, and he can rescue them easily.

Blessed is the person who trusts in the Lord.
classic_reading:
[2Chr.18.1]
Chapter 18
Jehoshaphat's alliance with Ahab.
--This history we read in 1Ki 22. Abundant riches and honour give large opportunities of doing good, but they are attended with many snares and temptations. Men do not know much of the artifices of Satan and the deceitfulness of their own hearts, when they covet riches with the idea of being able to do good with them. What can hurt those whom God will protect? What can shelter those whom God will destroy? Jehoshaphat is safe in his robes, Ahab killed in his armour; for the race is not to the swift, nor the battle to the strong. We should be cautious of entangling ourselves in the worldly undertakings of evil men; and still more we should avoid engaging in their sinful projects. But, when they call upon him, God can and will bring his faithful people out of the difficulties and dangers into which they have sinfully run themselves. He has all hearts in his hand, so that he easily rescues them. Blessed is the man that putteth his trust in the Lord.

modern_osis:
Original heading

Jehoshaphat visits his kingdom.

Jehoshaphat receives correction and reforms Judah

Whenever we return home safely, we should recognize that Providence preserved our coming and going.

After escaping unusual danger, we have special reason to give thanks.

Exceptional mercies create exceptional obligations.

A prophet plainly told Jehoshaphat that joining Ahab had been very wrong.

Jehoshaphat received the rebuke well.

Notice how it affected his conduct: he searched his kingdom carefully to identify what remained to be corrected.

The prophet's words also showed him that his earlier reforms had pleased God.

That encouraged him to complete what was unfinished.

It is good when commendation spurs us on toward greater faithfulness.

Different gifts and kinds of service come from the same Spirit and are given for the common good.

Everyone who has received a gift should use it to serve others.

We should thank God for judges and ministers, scholars and officials, people who work with books and people who work in practical affairs.

Jehoshaphat charged them to do everything in reverence for God, with sincere and upright hearts.

They were to work constantly to prevent sin, knowing that it offends God and can bring judgment upon the people.
classic_reading:
[2Chr.19.1]
Chapter 19
Jehoshaphat visits his kingdom.
--Whenever we return in peace to our houses, we ought to acknowledge God's providence in preserving our going out and coming in. And if we have been kept through more than common dangers, we are, in a special manner, bound to be thankful. Distinguishing mercies lay us under strong obligations. The prophet tells Jehoshaphat he had done very ill in joining Ahab. He took the reproof well. See the effect the reproof had upon him. He strictly searched his own kingdom. By what the prophet said, Jehoshaphat perceived that his former attempts for reformation were well-pleasing to God; therefore he did what was then left undone. It is good when commendations quicken us to our duty. There are diversities of gifts and operations, but all from the same Spirit, and for the public good; and as every one has received the gift, so let him minister the same. Blessed be God for magistrates and ministers, scribes and statesmen, men of books, and men of business. Observe the charge the king gave. They must do all in the fear of the Lord, with a perfect, upright heart. And they must make it their constant care to prevent sin, as an offence to God, and what would bring wrath on the people.

Judah faces danger and prays (verses 1–13)

In every danger, whether public or personal, our first response should be to seek God's help.

This is one benefit of days set aside for national fasting and prayer.

Throughout our approach to God, we must humble ourselves over our sins and rely upon his mercy and power alone.

Jehoshaphat acknowledged God's sovereign rule over all events and asked him to exercise it on Judah's behalf.

Whom else should they seek or trust for relief but the God they had chosen and served?

Those who use their possessions for God may hope confidently in his protection.

Every true believer is a child of Abraham and a friend of God, included in his eternal covenant and entitled to its promises.

God's love is assured to us because he has dwelt in human nature in the person of the Savior.

Jehoshaphat appealed to the temple as a sign of God's gracious presence.

He also described the injustice of his enemies.

We may appeal to God when people repay good with evil.

Though Jehoshaphat commanded a large army, he acknowledged, “We have no strength without you; we depend entirely on you.”

Jahaziel announces victory (verses 14–19)

The Spirit of prophecy came upon a Levite while the people were gathered together.

Like the wind, the Spirit acts where and upon whom he wills.

The message encouraged them to trust the Lord.

When a Christian soldier goes out against spiritual enemies, the God of peace will make that believer more than a conqueror.

Our trials can become our gain.

We receive the benefit, but all the glory belongs to God.

Judah celebrates deliverance (verses 20–30)

Jehoshaphat encouraged the troops to maintain firm faith in God.

Faith gives genuine courage.

Nothing more firmly establishes a heart during unstable and frightening times than confidence in God's power, mercy and promise.

In every act of trust and praise, we should especially remember his everlasting mercy toward sinners through Jesus Christ.

The invading forces destroyed one another in an extraordinary defeat.

God often allows wicked people to destroy one another.

Few victories have ever been celebrated with thanksgiving as solemn as Judah's was.

Jehoshaphat joins Ahaziah (verses 31–37)

Jehoshaphat remained devoted to God's appointed worship and worked to keep his people faithful.

But after God had granted him such remarkable gifts—not only victory, but wealth—his alliance with a wicked king was deeply ungrateful.

He should have expected the Lord's displeasure.

It appears, however, that he accepted the later warning.

When Ahaziah again pressed him to join in a project, Jehoshaphat refused (1 Kings 22:49).

The alliance ended, and God's rebuke produced a change, at least for a time.

Let us be thankful for losses that may have prevented the far greater loss of our immortal souls.

Praise the Lord, who sought us and did not leave us to perish in our sins.
classic_reading:
[2Chr.20.1-2Chr.20.13]
Chapter 20
Chapter Outline
The danger and distress of Judah. | (1-13) |
Jahaziel's prophecy of victory. | (14-19) |
The thanksgiving of Judah. | (20-30) |
Jehoshaphat's alliance with Ahaziah. | (31-37) |
Verses 1-13
In all dangers, public or personal, our first business should be to seek help from God. Hence the advantage of days for national fasting and prayer. From the first to the last of our seeking the Lord, we must approach him with humiliation for our sins, trusting only in his mercy and power. Jehoshaphat acknowledges the sovereign dominion of the Divine Providence. Lord, exert it on our behalf. Whom should we seek to, whom should we trust to for relief, but the God we have chosen and served. Those that use what they have for God, may comfortably hope he will secure it to them. Every true believer is a son of Abraham, a friend of God; with such the everlasting covenant is established, to such every promise belongs. We are assured of God's love, by his dwelling in human nature in the person of the Saviour. Jehoshaphat mentions the temple, as a token of God's favourable presence. He pleads the injustice of his enemies. We may well appeal to God against those that render us evil for good. Though he had a great army, he said, We have no might without thee; we rely upon thee.
[2Chr.20.14-2Chr.20.19]
Verses 14-19
The Spirit of prophecy came upon a Levite in the midst of the congregation. The Spirit, like the wind, blows where and on whom He listeth. He encouraged them to trust in God. Let the Christian soldier go out against his spiritual enemies, and the God of peace will make him more than a conqueror. Our trials will prove our gain. The advantage will be all our own, but the whole glory must be given to God.
[2Chr.20.20-2Chr.20.30]
Verses 20-30
Jehoshaphat exhorted his troops to firm faith in God. Faith inspires a man with true courage; nor will any thing help more to the establishing of the heart in shaking times, than a firm belief of the power, and mercy, and promise of God. In all our trust in the Lord, and our praises of him, let us especially look at his everlasting mercy to sinners through Jesus Christ. Never was an army so destroyed as that of the enemy. Thus God often makes wicked people destroy one another. And never was a victory celebrated with more solemn thanksgivings.
[2Chr.20.31-2Chr.20.37]
Verses 31-37
Jehoshaphat kept close to the worship of God, and did what he could to keep his people close to it. But after God had done such great things for him, given him not only victory, but wealth; after this, to go and join himself with a wicked king, was very ungrateful. What could he expect but that God would be angry with him? Yet it seems, he took the warning; for when Ahaziah afterward pressed him to join him, he would not, [1Kgs.22.49] 1Ki 22:49. Thus the alliance was broken, and the Divine rebuke had its effect, at least for a season. Let us be thankful for any losses which may have prevented the loss of our immortal souls. Let us praise the Lord, who sought after us, and left us not to perish in our sins.
